title: Mean-field theory of neural networks: from spikes to firing rates
abstract: Connecting microscopic neuronal spiking to macroscopic brain function is a central challenge in computational neuroscience. Firing-rate models provide a framework for addressing this problem by describing neuronal activity at an intermediate level between individual spikes and large-scale population dynamics. Here, we introduce the foundations of firing-rate descriptions, formalizing their definitions through temporal, population, and trial averaging. We discuss experimental evidence for firing rates, from the input-output transfer functions of individual neurons to the tuning curves of different neuronal populations. We then establish the connection between spikes and firing rates in single neurons and recurrently connected excitatory-inhibitory populations using mean-field approximation. We illustrate how collective dynamics emerge from neuronal interactions, including population stimulus-response curves and bistability induced by recurrent coupling, and brain rhythms arising from synaptic depression. We briefly review extensions and applications of firing-rate models to learning, seizure-like oscillatory activity, visual selectivity, phase-amplitude coupling in neural oscillations, and whole-brain modeling. Together, these examples illustrate how firing-rate models provide effective descriptions of neural activity, linking the dynamics of individual neurons to collective computations across scales.

title: Generative Design with Real-time Physics Explainability: Towards Product Definition in the Age of AI
abstract: In this article, we explore opportunities from using generative AI in mechanical engineering. On the one hand, generative methods based on invertible neural networks have been recently proposed for the solution of inverse design problems, allowing to infer design parameters from performance labels. On the other hand, generative AI models have shown that they can act as real time capable surrogates for physics based simulations. Here we suggest that these two streams should be combined in a unified framework, where INN are used to control the design process from the customer requirements perspective and the generative simulation of the systems physics adds a layer of explainability, why the proposed design fulfils the requirements. As generative design is prone to hallucinations, we propose uncertainty quantification to fend off physically infeasible requests. Finally, validation with classical tools is a requirement for generative design process. To demonstrate the capabilities of our novel generative design paradigm, we develop two interactive environments, one for airfoil design based on simulator data and one for the combustor design space exploration based on measured data.

title: Foundation Tensor Networks Generalize Across Quantum Lattice Systems
abstract: Neural quantum states and tensor networks have emerged as leading techniques for simulating quantum many-body systems. However, disordered systems remain extremely challenging in both frameworks as they require computation of the ground state for every realization of the disorder. Recently, neural quantum states have been used to construct foundation models that generate the ground state directly from the Hamiltonian. Still, they are hindered by the need to perform extensive sampling to estimate observables. To address these difficulties, we introduce the foundation tensor network (FTN), which uses a neural network to generate the tensor network representation of the ground-state wavefunction from the Hamiltonian. To accelerate training, we develop a technique, called \texttt{GridBP}, based on iterated one-dimensional belief propagation that reduces the cost of computing the energy expectation value to just two tensor contractions. We use FTNs to calculate the critical parameters of the glass transition in the quantum Edwards-Anderson model via finite-size scaling analysis. To facilitate rapid averaging, we use a moment-generating function to evaluate the order parameter, lowering the cost to a single tensor contraction. We obtain high-fidelity estimates for the critical parameters by averaging over 500,000 disorder realizations.

title: Learning and Generating Time Trajectories of Multidimensional Stochastic Processes
abstract: We present a multidimensional statistics-informed neural network (SINN) framework for learning and generating trajectories of multicomponent stochastic processes. SINN is built upon a deterministic recurrent neural network that takes streams of white-noise sequences as input and generates ensembles of stochastic trajectories whose statistical properties match those of the underlying stochastic dynamics. While SINN has been demonstrated for various one-dimensional non-Markovian processes, extending it to multidimensional processes is essential for real-world applications. Here, we present key developments toward this goal. First, because direct estimation of multivariate probability density functions (PDFs) becomes computationally challenging with increasing dimension, we represent joint-distribution information using collections of one-dimensional PDFs constructed from linear combinations of the process components. Second, to accommodate the larger set of statistical objectives required to characterize multidimensional processes, we adopt a self-adaptive loss-balancing strategy that dynamically weights the components of the total loss function. Third, we introduce a reference-normalized validation framework that interprets statistical discrepancies relative to the finite-sample variability between independent target ensembles. We also investigate the role of the input white-noise dimension in SINN performance. We evaluate the proposed approach using a Langevin benchmark based on two coupled Duffing oscillators and further demonstrate its applicability to the Langevin dynamics of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam chain and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of a lattice Lotka-Volterra model. Our results demonstrate that the multidimensional SINN framework provides a practical approach for modeling multidimensional stochastic dynamics.

title: ADfiRe: An empirical- and CFD-informed advection-diffusion-reaction thermal model for wildfire spread
abstract: Real-time wildfire forecasting requires a trade-off between rapid yet physically relevant models and high fidelity but computationally costly models of flame spread over heterogeneous, multiphase solid fuel. The present study introduces ADfiRe, a hybrid framework that integrates empirical correlations and CFD-informed parameterizations into a physics-based advection-diffusion-reaction (ADR) formulation. The key features of ADfiRe are the use of established fuel databases, the capacity to handle multiple fuels, and a methodology to capture the effect of arbitrary topography. Furthermore, it includes the effect of flame tilting due to wind, thus accounting for the differences between plume- and wind-dominated fire propagation. ADfiRe resolves explicitly the coupled thermochemical degradation as well as heat and mass transport mechanisms of the advancing fire front. The wind field is modeled based on an appropriately defined Byram number. The model is validated against five well-documented experimental field-scale fires in Mediterranean shrublands, showing quantitative agreement with key metrics such as the rate of spread (ROS) and the fireline intensity, through a two-stage, Arrhenius-based heterogeneous reaction scheme coupling solid-fuel pyrolysis and oxygen-limited char/volatile combustion.

title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials
abstract: One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.

title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

title: Reconciling global and local spin models
abstract: Magnetic interactions based on first-principles calculations can be casted either into global spin models, where the interactions are configuration-independent, or into local spin models, where the effective parameters depend explicitly on the underlying spin configuration. Although these two perspectives often yield seemingly inconsistent results, we demonstrate that they can be reconciled by restricting the analysis to transverse spin fluctuations. We develop a projection scheme that systematically removes spurious longitudinal contributions from local interaction matrices, thereby establishing a rigorous connection between the projected local interactions and the underlying global multispin Hamiltonian. Applying our approach to the prototype systems (i) a Cr trimer on Au(111) (ii) Fe and Cr dimers on Cu(001), we show that the projected local interaction parameters quantitatively reproduce those obtained from the global four-spin model. This work provides a unified framework to interpret local and global spin models on equal footing and resolves long-standing ambiguities in the identification of effective interactions such as the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in a non-collinear framework.

title: CGTransformer: A Topology-Aware Autoregressive Framework for Crystal Generation and Inverse Design
abstract: Autoregressive language models offer a unified route to crystal generation and inverse design, but their performance depends on how periodic structures are serialized. Symmetry equivalent and closely related crystals can receive different atomic orders under coordinate-based serialization, introducing variability unrelated to their structural connectivity. Here, we present CGTransformer (Crystal Graph Transformer), an autoregressive generative framework that addresses this challenge via a graph-embedded sorting strategy. Using quotientgraph topology and barycentric embeddings, Element Symmetry Graph (ESG) converts periodic crystal networks into topology-guided one-dimensional sequences that retain key local and symmetry-related structural information. CGTransformer achieves high generation validity and the highest single shot crystal structure prediction (CSP) match rate among the compared MP-20 baselines (63.24%), while same backbone comparisons show improved structure recovery over coordinate-based ordering. Furthermore, we demonstrate property-conditioned inverse design for wide-bandgap semiconductors, where ESG achieves a much higher stable, unique and novel (S.U.N.) rate and stronger target-property alignment than the coordinate-based baseline. These results establish topology-guided sequence construction as an effective route to improving crystal generation and property-directed design at fixed model capacity.

title: Potential Flow, Stress, and Straightness in Flow Matching: Euler Error on Gaussian-Mixture Targets
abstract: In linear flow matching, coupling straightness measures conditional displacement variance. The conditional covariance gives a kinetic stress in the Jeans balance. The virial identity relates the mean trace of the covariance to a radial moment of acceleration. Euler error also depends on how the flow propagates acceleration. On constructed Gaussian-mixture targets, closed-form couplings with matched straightness yield different median Euler errors. Learned fields from fresh minibatch assignments also yield different Euler errors from their partners at matched estimated straightness. The leading Euler coefficient accounts for more of the error variation than straightness in these experiments. We relate the additive-noise characterization of isotropic Gaussian sources to potential flow. A gradient constraint reduces velocity error on the independent isotropic Gaussian example and increases it on two examples with rotational exact fields.

title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
authors: Andres Felipe Usuga (Centre of Excellence ENSEMBLE3 Sp. z o. o)
Ihor Radchenko (Centre of Excellence ENSEMBLE3 Sp. z o. o)
College of Chemical Engineering - Fuzhou University)
Centre of Excellence ENSEMBLE3 Sp. z o. o)
abstract: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

title: Verifying the High-Energy Tail in Bi-Kappa Particle Loading: Three-Dimensional Tests, Velocity Bounds, and Finite Precision
abstract: The bi-Kappa distribution models anisotropic space-plasma populations with suprathermal power-law tails. Kinetic simulations represent such a population by computational particles, and a loader draws their velocities from the requested bi-Kappa distribution, which we call the target distribution. When $\kappa$ is close to 1/2, floating-point underflow can remove the largest draws, and a velocity bound changes the loaded distribution. Published Kappa loaders are usually verified by comparing histograms of the speed or of one velocity component with the analytic distribution. Such comparisons do not examine the direction of the velocity or whether the direction is independent of the speed. We build an anisotropic loader on an established Gamma-ratio construction and examine each of these problems. Near $\kappa=1/2$, evaluating the Gamma ratio on a logarithmic scale avoids the loss of draws to underflow in single and double precision down to $\kappa=0.5001$. When draws outside a bound on each velocity component are discarded and redrawn, a small rejected fraction can accompany a large change in the tail. At $\kappa=2$ and $\theta_\parallel=2\theta_\perp$, a bound at 20 times each component's thermal speed rejects a fraction $3.6\times10^{-4}$ of the draws and lowers the 99.9th-percentile speed by 11%. We test the loaded velocities through their direction and their normalized radius, the length of the velocity after each component is divided by $\sqrt{\kappa}$ times its thermal speed. The tests used nine values of $\kappa$ from 0.51 to 10, including $1/2<\kappa\le3/2$, where the second moments do not exist, with $\theta_\parallel=2\theta_\perp$ in double precision. At every $\kappa$, $\chi^2$ tests find the normalized radius out to its 99.999th percentile, the direction, and their joint distribution consistent with the target distribution.

title: Restoring Consistency with Poynting's Theorem in Numerical MHD and RMHD
abstract: For perfectly conducting plasmas, Poynting's theorem states that the time rate of change of electromagnetic energy density equals the negative of the divergence of the Poynting flux. To the best of our knowledge, this involutive theorem has never been mimetically incorporated in codes. We show that there is an inconsistency in MHD and RMHD codes that evolve face-centered magnetic fields in globally-divergence-free fashion. This is because the face-centered flux of energy density, which incorporates a Poynting vector, is evaluated using one-dimensional Riemann solvers that are applied at face-centers. However, the face-centered magnetic fields are evolved according to edge-centered electric fields that come from two-dimensional Riemann solvers that are applied to the edges of a zone. While edge-centered electric fields are used to evolve the magnetic field, they have no influence on the face-centered Poynting flux. For situations where the magnetic energy is much larger than the thermal energy, this causes a negative pressure to be evaluated at the zone-centers. This paper restores consistency by using edge-centered variables to evaluate a face-centered Poynting flux. A simple accuracy-preserving correction is made to the face-centered flux of energy density. We show that it helps considerably in simulations that have very strong magnetic fields.

title: A Surrogate Boundary Condition for Improved Accuracy and Performance of Local Modeling in Radiation Transport Simulations
abstract: Monte Carlo neutronics analysis of tokamak designs is computationally expensive due to the complex CAD geometries required to accurately model them. Design iteration of port plugs using global transport in the full model is impractical because of the computational cost. To circumvent this, local modeling methods are used. In the local modeling method, a boundary condition is assumed on the port plug, such that particles that leave the port plug do not require transport in the surrounding global model. For this purpose, vacuum and reflective boundaries are assumed, both of which provide poor approximation of the true transport physics in the global model. To improve on current techniques, a surrogate model is presented that provides a physics-informed boundary condition for the component. A neural network is trained to reproduce the boundary condition on the component that represents the behavior of particles returning from the surrounding geometry. Monte Carlo transport is only necessary within the component, and approximate physics from the surrounding region are retained. This approach allows the design in the component to be iterated without requiring full model transport and joining of the component mesh to the global mesh in each iteration. In this work, the surrogate model is evaluated against vacuum and reflective boundaries-- outperforming both in accuracy, with surrogate predictions of the flux in the port plug differing less than 12% from the global transport solution in any given energy bin. The surrogate boundary condition is also demonstrated to be more performant than global transport for the simplified benchmark geometry.
